verdicts.reason: Cal's fear that a cold, inborn wickedness runs in his blood comes from his mother really being this kind of person. Without her nature, the truth he carries would not frighten him about himself, and it would not be so terrible to show Aron.
Cal never learns of the betrayal with Charles. Nothing in his motives or self-image at the reveal depends on it.
The birth and Cathy's indifference to the babies are details Cal never knows. They do not shape what he believes or wants at the reveal.
Her abandonment makes Cal a motherless boy raised on a lie, with a hidden mother he has to discover. This is the wound underneath his hunger to be loved.
Adam's story to the deputy is not the lie Cal grows up with; the secrecy that shapes Cal is kept up by later choices. Cal at the reveal is the same without this scene.
The weapon Cal uses is that their mother is a Salinas brothel madam. Without Kate, there is nothing to show Aron.
Lee becoming Cal's real parent while Adam stays distant shapes Cal's need for his father's love and his trust in Lee's counsel.
The blow mainly moves the plot toward the naming and Adam's slow recovery. It does not itself shape Cal's feelings or reasons at the reveal.
Cal never knows how the naming debate went. The ideas that reach him come through Lee's later teaching, not through this scene.
The speech explains Cal's act thematically, but Cal never hears it. He would strike back out of rejection just the same.
Through Lee, Cal comes to believe his acts are his own and not his mother's blood. So he does the deed knowing he chose it, which feeds his guilt.
This informs Adam, not Cal. Cal's discovery of Kate comes on its own path.
Adam's release moves the family forward toward Salinas and later ventures. Cal's motives at the reveal come from other events.
Cal first feels that people naturally love Aron more, and his jealous meanness shows itself. That resentment drives the reveal.
Cal learns his mother may be alive and already uses the hint to hurt Aron. It sets up both his search for her and his habit of using her as a weapon.
Cal's fear that he is mean by nature, and his longing to be loved like Aron, frame how he takes his mother's identity and his own cruelty.
Cal's plan to restore his father's lost money exists because of this loss. Without the gift there is no rejection to set off the reveal.
Aron's fragile purity is exactly what Cal knows the truth will shatter. It also earns Aron the father's pride that Cal envies.
Without knowing Kate is his mother, Cal has no secret to turn on Aron.
Lee tells Cal he has his father in him too and is responsible for what he does. Cal acts as a free agent rather than as his mother's son, which shapes his guilt.
Having faced Kate and lost his fear of her, Cal knows the house and can lead Aron into it. Without this he could not stage the confrontation as he does.
Adam's burden over the boys he sends to war is why he spurns Cal's war-profit money. That rejection sends Cal to Kate's that night.
The bean venture is Cal's bid to earn his father's love. Its rejection is what drives him to the reveal.
The loan mostly supplies the money for the deal. Cal's feelings at the reveal come from the plan and its rejection, not from where the money came from.
Watching his father glow over Aron deepens Cal's sense of being the overlooked son. That sharpens the jealousy behind the reveal.
Aron's departure mainly arranges the Thanksgiving homecoming. Cal's jealousy and hope are already in place.
Cal's high hope that this gift will win his father's love is what makes the refusal crushing enough to drive him to strike at Aron.
The rejection, with Aron held up as the son Adam wants, is the direct trigger of Cal's revenge that night.
Lee's attempt to steady him does not reach Cal. He goes to Kate's with the same rage and the same reasons.
This is the focal event: Cal strikes at his favored brother by showing him their mother.
